deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no derivations, computations or formulas. It is a set of aphoristic philosophical-methodological notes from Hilbert's notebook. Internal evidence dates them to about 1912-13: the adjacent page quotes Einstein's letter to Sommerfeld of 29.10.1912.

The first line continues a sentence that ends on the page supplied as the 'next' page: "Eine Art Ω-These: man kann die Gesetze der Wahrscheinlichkeit auf Logik und mathematische Behauptungen (z.B. Max-" | "wellscher statistischer Grundprinzip der Mittelwertbildung, √2 ist irrational, in π-Decimalbruchentwickelung kommen 1en und 2en asymptotisch gleich oft vor etc.) mit demselben Recht u. Erfolg wie auf Erfahrungsthatsachen anwenden." So the leaves are out of order relative to the supplied context, or recto and verso are interchanged.

In modern terms the 'Ω-thesis' says that probabilistic laws may be applied to mathematical propositions just as to empirical facts. The examples are:
(a) Maxwell's statistical averaging principle, i.e. the ergodic/mean-value assumption of kinetic theory;
(b) the irrationality of √2;
(c) the conjecture that the digits 1 and 2 occur asymptotically equally often in the decimal expansion of π. For a digit d this reads lim_{N→∞} #{n ≤ N : d_n(π) = d}/N = 1/10, the frequency part of the (still open) simple normality of π.

The remaining notes are:
1. All simplest propositions (those of logic) are alike, i.e. there are only few of them, just as all simplest bodies (electrons) are alike.
2. The pre-established harmony between thinking and being must have a deeper ground, to be found; it shows in simplicity of theory and experiment and in reality agreeing with beautiful, simple theories. Hilbert calls this a philosophical problem.
3. Unlike thermodynamics, where heat and energy degrade, in the intellectual realm things improve, refine and differentiate with age.
4. All striving presupposes that there is only one correct opinion (monism).
5. The axiomatic method is the general form of thought, also for philosophers and parliamentarians. Only the material differs: for mathematicians it is the world of numbers, elsewhere facts and sensations.
6. 'Proof of all proofs': that one must always be able to find the proof. This is the solvability/no-ignorabimus thesis.

None of these is derived; they are programmatic statements.
errors: No mathematical errors, since no derivations are given.

The claim that the digits 1 and 2 occur asymptotically equally often in π is stated as an example of a mathematical assertion to which probability applies. It was unproven then and remains unproven: normality, even simple normality, of π is open.
Grammatically the first line reads 'wellscher statistischer Grundprinzip' (sic), mixing genders. It is a hasty note.

deep.surprise_reason: Most items are well-known Hilbertian themes: pre-established harmony, axiomatic thinking, no ignorabimus, monism. The mildly notable element is the explicit 'Ω-thesis' of applying probability laws to mathematical statements, with π's digit frequencies as an example, around 1912-13. It is an early private formulation of probabilistic heuristics for mathematical truths, but it is only a programmatic aside without content.
